prompt: I run a little booking site for community repair cafes (people bring broken toasters, lamps, bike lights, that kind of thing and volunteers fix them with you). The site is called Tern & Wick. Can you build the first screen of the homepage? Headline idea: 'Don't bin it. Bring it in.' Under it: 'Book a 30-minute slot at a repair cafe near you. Volunteers, tools and tea are free.' I want people to book a slot, but I also want a link for 'How a repair cafe works' for the nervous first-timers. Little line at the bottom: '214 cafes in 9 countries, 41,000 things fixed'. One self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets.
rubric: The headline is clearly the first thing the eye lands on; nothing else on the screen competes with it for size or weight.
There is exactly one visually dominant button, 'Book a slot' or equivalent, and the 'How a repair cafe works' link is clearly quieter than it yet still findable.
The supporting sentence and the stats line are visibly subordinate to the headline, and the stats line is the quietest text on the screen.
There are at least three distinguishable levels of emphasis (headline, supporting text, small print) with visible steps between them rather than near-identical sizes.
Decoration (shapes, gradients, icons, shadows) is sparse and does not pull attention away from the headline or the main button.

prompt: Build me a pricing section for Hushcast, a podcast hosting service. Three plans: Starter at $9/month (1 show, 5 hours of audio a month, basic stats), Studio at $24/month (5 shows, 30 hours, detailed stats, ad-free embeds, custom domain) and Network at $79/month (unlimited shows, 200 hours, team seats, priority support). Studio is the one we really want people to pick and it's what most customers buy. Put a heading on it too. Single HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, nothing loaded from outside.
rubric: Studio is recognisably the recommended plan through more than one cue (for example a label, a stronger border or fill, a filled button) while still looking like it belongs with the other two.
In each card the price is the most prominent text, ahead of the plan name and the feature list.
The Starter and Network cards remain readable and have a usable button but are visibly quieter than Studio's.
The feature lists are scannable: short lines, consistent alignment, no feature text competing with the price or the button.
The section heading is clearly above the cards in the order of emphasis but does not outshout the recommended plan.

prompt: Make the empty state for the 'Saved routes' tab in our cycling app, Spokeline. A new rider opens it and has nothing saved yet. What we want: explain in one line what saving a route does (it keeps the route for offline use and shows it on their watch), and get them to start by importing a route file or picking one from the 'Popular nearby' list. Mobile-width screen, about 390px wide, with the tab bar at the bottom (Home, Saved routes, Record, Profile) and 'Saved routes' as the active tab. Single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts, no external images.
rubric: One action is clearly the main one on the screen; the second path (import vs. popular nearby) is present but visibly secondary.
A short headline and the one-line explanation are readable and ranked: headline first, explanation second.
Any illustration or icon is modest and does not outweigh the headline or the main action.
The bottom tab bar is quiet, with the active tab distinguishable from the others without being louder than the empty-state content.
The content block is grouped and centered or aligned in one consistent way instead of scattered across the screen.

prompt: We grow gourmet mushrooms and I built a little monitoring page for the grow rooms. It shows 8 cards in a 4x2 grid, one per room. Every card has the same white background, same light-grey border, same soft shadow, and the same layout: room name in 14px bold, then temperature, humidity, CO2 and 'days to harvest' as four equal 28px bold numbers with small grey labels. When a room is out of range the only difference is that the number turns a slightly darker orange, and there's a tiny 'alert' word in 11px grey in the corner. Last week Room 5's humidity sat at 61% for six hours and nobody noticed. My co-founder says the page 'feels flat'. What's actually wrong and what should I change first?
rubric: Names the real problem: nothing separates the rooms that need attention from the ones that don't, so an out-of-range room is lost among 8 identical cards (not just 'it needs more color').
Connects the diagnosis to the Room 5 incident rather than giving generic advice.
Gives a prioritized fix order with the first change being to make out-of-range readings or rooms stand out clearly.
Proposes making the in-range state quieter (not only making the alert louder), so contrast comes from restraint as well as emphasis.
Says what to keep or leave alone (for example the consistent card structure or the readable labels) rather than recommending a full redesign.
Concrete enough to act on: describes the actual treatment (what changes in size, weight, fill or position), not just 'improve hierarchy'.

prompt: We have a small invoicing app for freelancers. On the main Invoices screen three messages can show at the same time: (1) 'Your card ending 4417 was declined. Your plan will pause on 14 March unless you update it.' (2) 'New: you can now send invoices in Portuguese.' (3) 'Tip: press N to start a new invoice.' Right now all three are the same blue banner stacked at the top, and people ignore all of them. How loud should each one be, and where should each go? I want something I can hand to my developer.
rubric: The declined-card message is clearly the most prominent of the three, and the answer says why (it has a deadline and consequence).

The Portuguese announcement and the shortcut tip are treated as clearly quieter than the payment message, and the answer gives them different treatments from each other (for example a dismissible notice vs. a small inline hint) rather than the same one.
Gives a concrete treatment and placement for each message (colour or fill intensity, position, whether it is dismissible, whether it has an action), usable as a developer handoff.
Does not recommend a full-screen takeover or blocking modal for the payment issue; it stays loud enough to notice while leaving the invoices usable.
The payment banner includes a direct action (such as 'Update card') as its single primary control.
Delivers revised HTML/CSS that is coherent and would run, not only a description of changes.
'Reserve a seat' is the one clearly emphasised button; 'Add to wishlist' and 'Share' are visibly demoted (for example to text or outline style).
Shadows, borders and gradients are cut back so the card has no more than a couple of separate decorative effects, and the answer explains why the removed ones were not pulling their weight.
The class title is clearly the top text level, with price and meta/seat info ranked below it by something other than 'everything bold'.
Keeps the useful signals (NEW, seats left) but makes them proportionate rather than competing with the title and button.
Does not invent new content, features or sections that were not in the original card.

prompt: My landing page for a bookkeeping tool for dog groomers looks like every other startup page and I don't know why. It has a centered hero with a pill that says 'New: AI-powered' in a purple-to-pink gradient, a big headline with a gradient fill, a glowing purple shadow under the main button, then a row of three identical cards each with a gradient icon tile, a bold title and two lines of grey text, and the same three-card pattern again further down for pricing. Every section has a soft blob shape in the background. What's making it feel generic, and what would make it feel like it's ours?
rubric: Explains the generic feel in specific terms tied to the elements the user listed (the pill, gradient headline, glow, repeated identical cards, blobs) instead of saying 'it's too common'.
Identifies that the repeated identical treatment (same cards, same effects everywhere) leaves no clear focal point or step between levels.
Says which decorations to drop or keep and why, judging each by whether it helps the reader find the main message or action.
Suggests changes that come from the product's own content or audience (groomers, appointments, dogs, money) rather than a different generic style.
Gives an order of what to change first, and is not a rewrite of the whole page or a list of ten unrelated tips.

prompt: I'm redesigning the main screen of a dispatch board for a freight yard. Dispatchers sit in front of it all shift. It has to show every truck currently on site, usually 40 to 60 at once, with: truck ID, carrier, dock door, status (arriving, waiting, loading, unloading, ready to leave), minutes on site, and a notes column. Right now it's a plain table and the dispatchers say it's overwhelming, but they refuse to scroll or page through it or hide any trucks. Lay out the screen for me. I'm thinking of a big hero stat at the top and bigger cards for the most important trucks, what do you think?
rubric: Keeps all trucks visible at once in a compact, scannable structure and does not accept paging, hiding or large cards that would force scrolling.
Does not push a single hero stat or one giant focal element onto a screen that is meant to be scanned continuously; it explains why, or limits any summary to a thin, quiet strip.
Makes normal rows quiet and uniform, and makes exceptions (for example trucks waiting too long or blocked) stand out through a small number of strong signals.
Uses consistent alignment and column order so the eye can run down a column, and describes how status is encoded without relying on many competing colors.
Responds directly to the user's hero-stat and bigger-cards idea instead of ignoring it.

prompt:
Before I hand this to the developer, can you look over the layout of our Notifications settings page and tell me if anything needs changing? Here's how it's built:

- Page title 'Notifications' at 28px semibold, with a one-line grey description under it.
- Three sections: 'Email', 'Push' and 'Weekly summary'. Each has an 18px semibold heading, and below it a list of rows. A row has the setting name (16px regular), a grey 14px explanation underneath, and a switch on the right.
- Rows are separated by thin light lines. Sections are separated by generous extra space.
- The switches use the brand teal when on and grey when off. Nothing else on the page is teal.
- At the bottom, a single teal 'Save changes' button, aligned left with the content, with a plain text 'Reset to defaults' link next to it.
- No icons, no shadows, no cards. White background.
rubric: Concludes that the hierarchy already works, and says so plainly instead of hunting for problems.
Names specific things that are working (for example clear title/section/row levels, a single accent colour, one primary action, restrained separators).
Makes no more than one or two minor suggestions and marks them as optional or low-priority.
Does not recommend adding cards, icons, shadows, banners, extra colour or bigger type to make the page look more designed.
Does not invent defects that are not in the description.

prompt: On our bakery's order page the last step has two buttons: 'Place order' and 'Back to cart'. Which should be the filled, prominent one? Answer in two sentences at most.
rubric: Picks 'Place order' as the filled, prominent button and 'Back to cart' as the quieter one.
Gives a reason in terms of what the visitor is trying to do or the cost of a mistake.
Stays within two sentences, about 50 words or fewer, with no headings or bullet lists.
Does not pad the answer with extra suggestions about colour, shadows or other redesign.
